what_it_does: Helps reduce the look of excess pigmentation and uneven tone.
summary_short: Tranexamic acid is used in skincare mainly for melasma and dark spots. It works by helping interrupt pigment-triggering pathways linked to inflammation and UV exposure, and is often paired with sunscreen and other brightening ingredients.
summary_long:
Tranexamic acid is a synthetic derivative of lysine best known medically as an antifibrinolytic, meaning it helps reduce bleeding by blocking plasmin formation. In skin, that same plasmin-related pathway appears to influence inflammation, blood-vessel signaling, and pigment production, which is why tranexamic acid is now used in dermatology for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [PMID:unknown].

For skincare users, its main role is tone-evening rather than exfoliation. It is thought to help suppress melanogenesis, the process that creates melanin, and may also reduce inflammatory and vascular signals that can worsen discoloration. This makes it especially relevant for melasma, acne marks, and other forms of stubborn pigmentation [PMID:unknown].

The strongest dermatology interest is in melasma, where tranexamic acid has been studied by oral, topical, and intradermal routes. Cosmetic products use the topical route, which is generally more appropriate for routine skincare than oral use. Oral tranexamic acid is a prescription medical treatment in many contexts and has clot-related safety considerations, so it should not be treated like an ordinary cosmetic brightener.

Topical tranexamic acid is commonly found in leave-on serums and creams, often alongside niacinamide, licorice-derived brighteners, kojic acid, alpha arbutin, azelaic acid, or gentle exfoliating acids. Daily sunscreen is an important pairing because UV and visible light can keep pigmentation pathways active.

It is not an exfoliating acid in the AHA/BHA sense, despite the word “acid” in its name. It is usually positioned as a gentler brightening ingredient, though irritation can still happen depending on the full formula, especially when combined with strong acids, retinoids, or high-strength vitamin C.
quick_facts: Oral use is medical, not cosmetic
